title: Peasant, Worker and Revolutionary Movements

cards.b:
The mainstream story centres on Congress leaders. But peasants, tribals, workers and young revolutionaries made their own movements, with their own demands. Sometimes they joined the national movement. Sometimes they ran ahead of it, or against it.

The syllabus puts three streams together: peasant, worker and revolutionary movements. Examiners ask how these fed the national movement and how they tested its leadership, which was largely middle class and wary of class conflict.

Learn this lesson in three parts: peasants (and tribals), workers, and revolutionaries. For each, know the key events, leaders, methods, outcomes and a one-line judgment. Link to Subaltern Studies and Marxist readings.

Early peasant action was local, spontaneous and aimed at specific exploiters: planters, moneylenders and zamindars. Most did not question British rule itself.

  • Indigo revolt (Bengal, 1859-60): peasants refused to grow indigo under forced contracts. Dinabandhu Mitra's play Nil Darpan (1860) exposed the planters. The Indigo Commission followed.
  • Pabna agrarian leagues (1873-76, Bengal): resistance to rent increases. Led by Ishan Chandra Roy.
  • Deccan riots (1875): peasants attacked moneylenders in Pune and Ahmednagar. The Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act came in 1879.
  • Tribal revolts: Santhal hul (1855-56, Sidhu and Kanhu), and the Munda ulgulan led by Birsa Munda (1899-1900), against outsiders and land alienation.

These show that agrarian grievances in colonial India came from revenue systems, debt and commercialisation.

• Awadh Kisan Sabha (1920, Baba Ramchandra, with Nehru's help): against evictions and extra dues. Eka movement (1921-22) followed.
  • Moplah revolt (Malabar, 1921): tenants against landlords, mixed with Khilafat feeling; it turned communal in places.
  • Bardoli (1928): Vallabhbhai Patel led a no-tax campaign against a rise in land revenue, and won; he gained the title "Sardar".
  • Kisan Sabhas: Swami Sahajanand Saraswati founded the Bihar Provincial Kisan Sabha (1929). The All India Kisan Sabha was set up in Lucknow in April 1936, with N.G. Ranga and others. It demanded abolition of zamindari. Its tensions with Congress deepened in the late 1930s.

• Tebhaga (Bengal, 1946-47): sharecroppers demanded two-thirds of the crop, not half. Led by the Kisan Sabha and communists.
  • Telangana (1946-51): against the Nizam's landlords (jagirdars and deshmukhs). The Communist Party led an armed struggle. It continued after Hyderabad's accession (Operation Polo, September 1948) and was withdrawn in 1951.
  • Punnapra-Vayalar (Kerala, 1946) and the Warli revolt (Maharashtra, 1945-47).

Outcome: Peasant pressure shaped the Congress agrarian programme (Karachi 1931, the Faizpur session of December 1936) and led to zamindari abolition after independence. The First Amendment (1951) and the Ninth Schedule protected land reform laws.

Limits: middle-class Congress leaders feared class war and landlord support. Gandhi preferred reconciliation of classes, not conflict. Marxists say this blunted radical land reform.

cards.h: The working class and trade unions
cards.b:
• Early phase: philanthropic efforts by individuals such as N.M. Lokhande (Bombay Mill Hands Association, 1890). Strikes followed the Swadeshi movement (1905-08) and Tilak's trial (1908) in Bombay.
  • After 1918: strikes grew with post-war inflation. B.P. Wadia founded the Madras Labour Union (1918). Gandhi guided the Textile Labour Association in Ahmedabad (1920).
  • AITUC was founded in Bombay in October 1920, with Lala Lajpat Rai as the first president.
  • Legal change: Trade Unions Act, 1926 (registration, legal status); Trade Disputes Act, 1929 (limits on strikes); Royal Commission on Labour, 1929-31.
  • Communist influence: the Communist Party of India (1925), the Workers and Peasants Parties and the Girni Kamgar Union led the Bombay textile strike (1928). The Meerut Conspiracy Case (1929-33) tried 31 labour leaders.
  • After independence: INTUC (May 1947), HMS (1948), and UTUC (1949).

cards.h: Did the Congress and workers/peasants pull together?
cards.b:
• Link: the Congress needed their numbers, and mass campaigns drew on rural resentment. The Karachi resolution (1931) promised fundamental rights and relief for workers and peasants.
  • Distance: the Congress stood for national unity across classes. Business groups such as Tata and Birla helped fund it. Fear of class conflict kept it from backing radical land redistribution or industrial strikes without limits.
  • Communists and socialists: the Congress Socialist Party (1934) pushed the Congress left. Communists cooperated, split and rejoined at different times. In 1942 they opposed Quit India after the USSR entered the war, which cost them credibility.
  • Subaltern view (Guha, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency, 1983): peasants had their own political consciousness. They used the nationalist leaders' names for their own ends.

The revolutionaries believed that British rule could end only by force. Their idea of the nation was often religious or heroic.

  • Maharashtra: Chapekar brothers killed Rand in Pune in 1897.
  • Bengal: Anushilan Samiti (1902) and Jugantar (Barindra Ghose). The Alipore Bomb Case (1908): Khudiram Bose was hanged; Aurobindo was acquitted in 1909. Rash Behari Bose took part in the Delhi bomb attack on Viceroy Hardinge (1912).
  • Abroad: India House in London (Shyamji Krishnavarma; Savarkar), Madame Cama in Paris and the Ghadar Party (1913, San Francisco; Lala Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna). The Komagata Maru incident (1914) and the failed Ghadar uprising of 1915 followed.

Main weakness: small, secret groups with no mass base, easily suppressed.

After Chauri Chaura and the end of non-cooperation, young people turned to a new idea: a revolution with a social aim.

  • HRA (1924, Kanpur): Ram Prasad Bismil, Sachindranath Sanyal, Jogesh Chatterjee. The Kakori train robbery (9 August 1925). Bismil, Ashfaqulla Khan, Roshan Singh and Rajendra Lahiri were hanged.
  • HSRA (September 1928, Delhi): socialist goals added. Members: Chandrashekhar Azad, Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Rajguru, Bhagwati Charan Vohra. They killed Saunders in Lahore (December 1928) to avenge Lajpat Rai. In April 1929 Bhagat Singh and B.K. Dutt threw bombs in the Central Assembly to "make the deaf hear". Jatin Das died on hunger strike in September 1929.
  • Chittagong armoury raid (18 April 1930): Surya Sen, with Ganesh Ghosh, Ananta Singh, and later Pritilata Waddedar.

Bhagat Singh was hanged on 23 March 1931 with Sukhdev and Rajguru. He wrote Why I Am an Atheist (1930).

• Gandhi's view: his 1930 article "The Cult of the Bomb" argued that violence was unsuitable for a mass struggle and would invite repression. Revolutionaries replied with Bhagwati Charan Vohra's "The Philosophy of the Bomb" (1930).
  • Role: the revolutionaries gave courage and inspired youth. Bhagat Singh's trial turned him into a national hero, as Nehru recorded.
  • Ideas: they moved from religious symbols to socialism and secularism, calling for "Inquilab Zindabad". Their goal was not just to end British rule but social revolution.
  • Limits: few members, no mass organisation, harsh crackdowns.

A balanced judgment: they did not defeat the Raj but they affected the national mood, and complemented rather than contradicted the mass movements.

• Agrarian: the farmers' agitation of 2020-21 against the three farm laws led to their repeal in November 2021. Kisan unions and a demand for legal MSP continue. The Land Acquisition Act, 2013, and the Forest Rights Act, 2006, are responses to old tribal and peasant grievances.
  • Labour: Parliament passed the four labour codes in 2019-20 (wages, industrial relations, social security, occupational safety). The Union government brought them into force on 21 November 2025, replacing 29 older laws. Unions have protested. Rules continue to be notified.
  • Left-wing extremism traces back to Naxalbari (1967), whose roots lie in the Telangana and Tebhaga traditions.
  • Memory: Bhagat Singh, Birsa Munda and others are celebrated in state commemorations, with fresh debate on their ideas.

"The peasant movements in colonial India were localised and reflected agrarian grievances more than anti-colonial sentiment." Discuss.
Assess the role of the working class in the national movement.
Examine the ideological transformation of the revolutionary movement from 1900 to 1931.
Why did the Congress leadership keep its distance from radical peasant and labour movements?

Structure: answer each stream in the same way: the cause, key events with years, leaders, relation to Congress, outcome, then an evaluation. Use the Subaltern and Marxist perspectives for analysis. Make a table of three streams (peasant, worker, revolutionary) with method and legacy. Add one present-day link such as the farm laws or labour codes.

quiz.q: Dinabandhu Mitra's play Nil Darpan (1860) was linked to…
quiz.w: It exposed planters' oppression of indigo cultivators.

quiz.q: The All India Kisan Sabha was formed in…
quiz.w: April 1936; Sahajanand Saraswati was first president.

quiz.q: The AITUC was founded in 1920 with which first president?

quiz.w: Thirty-one trade union leaders were tried.

The Chittagong armoury raid was led by…

o: Two-thirds of the crop for sharecroppers
quiz.w: Bengal sharecroppers demanded two-thirds, not half.
